records.text: 67. Component 2. Currently, neither Wajir nor Dadaab are recovering the full cost of water and sanitation services from consumers. County subsidies fill the gap. This is mainly due to the high cost of diesel to run the borehole pumps. In Dadaab, which serves the population through eight boreholes, about 90 percent of the average monthly revenues is used to pay for diesel. With the remaining 10 percent of the operating revenues, the cost for staff and repair and maintenance cannot be covered. In Wajir, the boreholes that rely solely on diesel generators incur higher costs than those which also draw on solar panels for energy. For example, in Khorof Harar, where pumps are powered by a mix of generators and solar panels, the water production cost was estimated to be KSh 22 per cubic meter, while at Haandaki which relies on the generators only, the production cost is KSh 44 per cubic meter.11 The WSDP will equip all boreholes in Wajir and Dadaab with solar panels. This is expected to reduce the cost of energy by about 50 percent, helping to make the operation of boreholes financially self-sustaining.

15. Short-term interventions under this component will focus on mitigating the impacts of water scarcity and drought and recurrence of waterborne diseases, particularly of cholera. They include treatment or chlorination of water from existing boreholes, rehabilitation of existing boreholes and equipping them with solar panels, and provision of water bowsers, plastic and collapsible tanks, and mobile water treatment units. In addition, the project will provide water meters and leak detection equipment to the WSPs to help them reduce NRW. Immediate interventions for Wajir town will include support to the Wajir cholera taskforce to review and implement the cholera control strategy and action plan.

18. Component 2 will also provide TA to the counties and their WSPs to build capacity to provide water and sanitation services. TA will focus on areas such as NRW reduction, billing and revenue collection systems, and developing and implementing a utility business plan. The component will also support activities to enable the Garissa WSP establish a regional office to serve the Dadaab host communities. Until the solar panels are installed at the boreholes (which will reduce the operating cost substantially), the project will also support the WSPs of Wajir and Garissa in financing part of their operating costs.

Public consultations of the RPF and ESMF were held in January 2017 with stakeholders from the six WSDP focus counties: Wajir, Garissa, Kwale, Mombasa, Kilifi, and Taita Taveta to discuss the contents of this RPF. In addition, the client conducted consultations in December 2016 on the site-specific safeguards instruments through public meetings and individual interviews with local officials. The results of the consultations are captured in the safeguards instruments. Overall, community members were supportive of the project and indicated that they hoped to see the completion of the works on time. Key stakeholders expressed concerns about the potential of political interference, not having a consultation process during implementation, the need to conduct water sources studies (that is, the Merti aquifer), odor issues at wastewater facilities, and clarification on compensation mechanisms, among others. Stakeholder feedback gathered through these workshops informed the final version of the SA and ESMF. These civil works will lead to environmental risks and social impacts, including health and safety concerns. Therefore, the Environmental Assessment assigned to this project is Category B. Because the scope and nature of most works as well as their specific locations are unknown at this stage of project preparation, the framework approach has been proposed, and the client has prepared an ESMF and an RPF. In addition, the client prepared ESIAs for subprojects that have sites/locations identified and detailed designs. The project will follow the World Bank Environmental, Health, and Safety Guidelines for Water and Sanitation. The ESMF and site-specific ESIAs have been publicly consulted upon and disclosed in-country and on the World Bank’s external website. Waterways On December 12, 2016, the Government of Kenya delivered a notification letter regarding the (OP/BP 7.50) project to the Government of Somalia through the Embassy of Somalia in Nairobi. Because of an error in the notification letter, the Government of Kenya sent a revised letter to the Embassy of Somalia and to Somalia’s Ministry of Water Resources on February 17 with a response date of March 6, 2017. No response has been received. The combined abstraction from the Merti aquifer is currently at 21,000 cubic meters per day. When the proposed water supply investments in Wajir town and Dadaab host communities are implemented there would be an increase in water abstraction of approximately 4,000 cubic meters per day, representing a 19 percent increment. Planned investments and aquifer abstraction decisions will be informed by recommendations of several ongoing technical studies, including the Merti aquifer assessment and management plan and a specific environmental and social impact assessment (ESIA) for the proposed activities. The studies will be made public and consultations will be conducted to get feedback from all stakeholders. The Regional Vice President cleared a memo summarizing the results of Riparian Notification under OP 7.50 on March 17, 2017.

Overall implementation progress is rated moderately satisfactory. Most of the preparatory activities required to be implemented before actual project implementation and disbursement, including the opening of designated/project accounts and establishment of Project Coordination Units (PCUs) by the different Implementing Agencies (IAs) have been completed. Significant progress has been made towards finalizing the County Participation Agreements (CPAs) between the National Treasury and Counties that will allow disbursement of funds to the counties and the Water Services Providers (WSPs). The Attorney General 's office provided clearance for CPAs for six counties under Component 1 and 2 - Wajir, Garissa, Kwale, Taita Taveta, Kilifi and Mombasa - together with their respective Water Services Providers (WSPs) Agreements in early May. The Agreements for Wajir and Garissa were signed by the Cabinet Secretary (CS)-MoWS and the respective counties on May 16, while those of the four Coast counties were signed on May 20. All the Agreements will be returned to the National Treasury (NT) for signature by the CS-NT, expected by May 24, after which the process will be completed. This represent a significant achievement to the sector and to the Project as it aligns the project implementation arrangement with the devolution of water and sanitation services delivery. Most of the Implementing Agencies have made good progress towards preparation of their proposed activities. The IAs have ready detailed designs and bidding documents for immediate interventions, and procurement has started for some of the activities. Two WSPs have awarded contracts amounting to US$6.5m, which will be signed once funds are transferred to the WSPs. Additional water supply and sanitation works contracts amounting to about US$20million are expected to be awarded by the end of June 2019. Most of the IAs have also advanced the procurement of consultancy firms to support them in design review, updating of safeguards documents and supervision of the immediate works contracts. Some IAs had slowed down the procurement process to avoid awarding contracts but not being able to commence because of unavailability of funds. With signing of the CPAs, implementation is expected to kick-off in earnest. To ensure their readiness to implement, the IAs have received significant capacity building and training in financial management, procurement and safeguards. Furthermore, the MoWS is in an advanced stage of procuring the services of a consulting firm that will provide practical and regular hands-on procurement, including on engineering, safeguards, procurement, financial management, as well as monitoring, evaluation and performance assessment services to ensure a successful implementation of the Project. This contract is expected to be signed by June 28, 2019.

Overall project implementation progress has been slow. However, efforts are been made to expedite implementation. In anticipation of receiving the funds, the counties and their water service providers (WSPs) have completed most of their preparatory activities—including establishment of Project Coordination Units (PCUs), opening of project accounts, and preparation of procurement plans. Adequate funds have been allocated in the Ministry of Water and Sanitation (MoWS) budget for financial year 2019/2020 for both the national and county-level implementing agencies (IAs) benefiting from components 1 and 2. In addition, the IAs have made good progress towards building a pipeline of implementable activities. Many have ready detailed designs and bidding documents for immediate interventions, although the pace of procurement has been slow owing to the uncertainty around the funds flow. Moreover, twelve IAs have initiated procurement of works, consultancy services, goods and non-consultancy services and some have awarded contracts (although no contracts can be signed until the funds expected under the project have been transferred to the WSPs). In addition, all the IAs have made good progress in the procurement of consulting firms to undertake design review and supervision of the immediate works contracts, and to prepare detailed designs for any additional identified medium and long-term interventions. IAs have received significant capacity building and training in financial management, procurement, and safeguards to ensure that once they receive funds, they can implement activities effectively. The MoWS is in an advanced stage of procuring the services of a consulting firm that will provide practical and regular technical assistance on procurement, engineering, safeguards, financial management, and monitoring, evaluation and performance assessment to ensure successful implementation of the project. This contract is expected to be signed soon. In addition, the County Participation Agreements (CPAs) and the Water Service Provider (WSP) Agreements were signed in June 2019, allowing disbursement to counties. Once the funds have been disbursed, implementation is expected to accelerate.

Overall project implementation progress has been slow. However, the main bottleneck of funds transfer to counties has been unlocked. All six counties under Component 1 and 2 received their first disbursement in their County Revenue Fund accounts at the end of December 2019. The counties subsequently transferred the funds to their water services providers (WSPs), which are in the process of making payments for signed contracts and reporting back on use of funds, before receiving additional funds. In addition, to further enhance and help accelerate implementation, some adjustments were made to the project’s institutional arrangements through the first restructuring that was approved by the Bank in January 2020 and is awaiting countersignature by the National Treasury. The implementing agencies (IAs) have continued to advance procurement of activities in their approved procurement plans. All the IAs have also made good progress in the procurement of consulting firms to undertake design review and supervision of the immediate works contracts, and to prepare detailed designs for any additional identified medium and long-term interventions. The IAs have received significant capacity building and training in financial management, procurement, and safeguards management to ensure that they can implement the project effectively. The MoWSI is expected to sign the contract for the framework consulting firm that will provide technical assistance to the IAs on procurement, engineering, safeguards, financial management, and monitoring, evaluation and performance assessment soon. This technical support will further enhance the capacity of the IAs as well as help to monitor and coordinate the project.

The project had a slow start due to multiple factors, including delays in meeting project effectiveness conditions, bottlenecks in funds flow processes, and the lack of implementation readiness for critical infrastructure investments. The project is the first World Bank-financed water and sanitation operation to be implemented under the devolved structure where counties and their water services providers (WSPs) are responsible for implementing county-specific project activities. In January 2020, at the request of the Government of Kenya (GoK), the World Bank approved a restructuring of the project involving, among others, adjustments to the project's institutional arrangements to accelerate implementation. The restructuring has helped to improve implementation progress. The main challenge of funds flow to the counties has been resolved. In addition, both the project steering committee and the technical committee have been constituted. In May 2020, the GoK requested a second restructuring to broaden the scope of the project to include interventions to strengthen the financial performance of WSPs affected by COVID-19 pandemic and to enhance their capacity to provide safe and reliable water services during and after the pandemic. Some US$50 million was reallocated to support a conditional liquidity grant facility. The restructuring has been completed and the grant is expected to be disbursed to WSPs between October and December 2020. Overall progress implementation has improved. The pace of implementation of project activities under Components 1 and 2 is picking up. To date, contracts worth about US$60 million (20 percent of the Credit) have been committed (signed/awarded). About half of these contracts are at the mobilization stage, although construction schedules have been affected by the current GoK restrictions related to the COVID-19 pandemic. Another set of contracts worth about US$40 million is at advanced stage of procurement, expected to be signed by end of October 2020. However, most of the implementing agencies (IAs) have encountered delays in awarding the contracts for consulting firms to undertake design review and supervision of the immediate works contracts, and to prepare detailed designs for any additional identified medium and long-term interventions. The technical assistance firm to be hired by MoWSI to support the IAs on key issues such as procurement, safeguards, financial management, evaluation M&E and performance assessment is also significantly delayed but is at the final stage of procurement. The IAs have continued to receive capacity building and training in key areas including financial management, procurement, and safeguards management to ensure that they can implement the project effectively.

The Project remains relevant to Kenya’s water and sanitation sector development agenda: it will support GoK’s Vision 2030 and the “Big Four” Agenda and it is also supporting the Government to mitigate the spread of the Covid-19 pandemic and in building community health resilience. The project has been restructured twice, to help address implementation bottlenecks and to respond to the Covid-19 pandemic. The first restructuring, completed in May 2020, has helped to improve implementation progress: the main challenge of funds flow to the counties was resolved and both the project steering committee and the technical committee were constituted and operationalized. The second restructuring was completed in August 2020 and the first tranche of the conditional liquidity grant in support of water service providers affected by the Covid-19 pandemic is expected to be disbursed in December 2020. Although the pace of implementation has picked up, the project remains substantially behind schedule. To date, contracts worth about US$60 million (20 percent of the Credit) have been committed (signed/awarded). About half of these contracts are at the mobilization stage, although construction schedules have been affected by GoK restrictions related to the Covid-19 pandemic. In addition, most of the implementing agencies have encountered delays in awarding the contracts for consulting firms to undertake design review and supervision of the immediate works contracts, and to prepare detailed designs for any additional medium and long-term interventions. This has further slowed the commencement of the awarded works contracts. It is assessed that some originally planned activities cannot be completed within the project timeframe. The World Bank and the Government of Kenya are discussing an action plan, which may involve a further project restructuring to align the project scope and targets to the project timeframe.

The Project remains relevant to Kenya’s water and sanitation sector development agenda: it will support GoK’s Vision 2030 and the “Big Four” Agenda and it is also supporting the Government to mitigate the spread of the Covid-19 pandemic. The project has been restructured three times. The first restructuring was to help address implementation bottlenecks. The second restructuring reallocated funds to assist WSPs that were negatively affected by economic shock caused by Covid-19. The third restructuring was undertaken following a formal request from National Treasury (NT) in February 2021 to align the project scope and revise results framework to reflect what is achievable within the remaining project timelines. Although the pace of implementation has picked up with both commitments and disbursements increasing, the project remains substantially behind schedule. All but one of the IAs have awarded the contracts for the consulting firms to undertake design review and supervision of the immediate works contracts, and to prepare detailed designs for any additional medium and long-term interventions. Some originally planned activities, such as the fecal sludge facilities for some IAs, will not be completed within the project timeframe. For these, the Project will support full preparation of detailed designs, bidding documents and safeguards documents so that they can be implemented should alternative financing be available.

Project implementation improved over the last six months following disbursements made to the Implementing Agencies that allowed for settling of pending bills and re-mobilization of contractors. The ripple effect of the delays is that whereas a good number of the 42 works contracts are expected to be completed within the project closing date, at least 33% are at high-risk of non-completion within the current timelines and would require very close monitoring at national and sub-national leadership levels.

Project implementation has remained steady despite continued challenges with timely enactment of the framework for disbursement of funds to the counties, leading to non-payment of contractors for extended periods of time. Some of the works contracts have been completed, with several others set to be completed over the next few months, subject to funds availability. Concerted efforts will however be required to rally the various contractors to resume works at optimal levels once funds are released and pending bills settled.

This ISR is done following an Implementation Support Mission conducted between January 14 to February 6, 2025. The overall progress has revealed marked improvement, with the mission noting that many contracts were in the close-out stages. Of a total of 45 contracts, 12 of them are now complete and intended populations have started to benefit. Some of these completed works already benefitting the people include sewer connections in Mombasa, water kiosks in Garissa, ablution blocks in Ukunda and Kwale town, and the office blocks in Kwale and Wajir counties that are providing improved working environment for staff and customer experience for the public. A further 25 works contracts are expected to be completed by August 2025. Some counties, however, posted mixed results. Construction of Fecal Sludge Treatment Facilities in Wajir and Kilifi and other contracts with a completion rate of less than 50 per cent are being closely monitored to ensure results are achieved within the project timeline. Due to delays in fund flows over the past three years and the limited financial capacity of some contractors, several Implementing Agencies have faced challenges resulting in slow progress of works and abandoned project sites. The County Government Additional Allocation Bill (CGAAB) for Financial Year 24/25 is yet to re-introduced for debate in Parliament as of February 10, 2024. Should the impasse continue, and funds not flow to the counties before April 2025, then the Project will be at very high risk of not completing works. The project completion date remains October 31, 2025, with no anticipated extension of the Project completion date.

The project has made significant progress in the completion of critical contracts needed to attain the project’s development objective. Overall physical progress of works contracts is at 85 percent, with 46 percent of works contracts and all goods contracts completed. Several of these completed works are already benefiting the intended beneficiaries including water distributions works in all seven WSPs in the Project, water kiosks in Garissa, ablution blocks in Ukunda, Kwale and Wajir towns, sewer connections in Mombasa and the Baricho bulk water supply scheme whose capacity has been expanded to serve Mombasa and Kilifi counties better and its resilience to flooding risks enhanced. The remaining works contracts are expected to be completed within the remaining project period. Grievances raised under the project are being closely monitored by both the Bank and the Ministry for their resolution ahead of the project closure.

The Project is making steady overall progress across its components. In the coastal region, bulk water supply capacity has been significantly enhanced through the rehabilitation of the Baricho water supply system, adding 36,000m³/day of supply capacity to Kilifi and Mombasa counties. Solarization of the Baricho bulk water system is complete and expected to deliver substantial energy cost savings estimated at Kshs 10 million per month. Water distribution and sanitation contracts are advancing well, with most works either completed or nearing completion. Sanitation infrastructure, including ablution blocks, sewer networks, and fecal sludge treatment plants, is largely on track. In the northeastern counties, rehabilitation and construction of boreholes and sanitation facilities in Garissa and Wajir are substantially complete or nearing finalization, and long-term water supply planning for Wajir county is advancing with key technical and hydrogeological deliverables are being finalized. At the national level, the Conditional Liquidity Support Grant is rolling out activities aimed at supporting the financial recovery of Water Service Providers. The Utility Turnaround Framework has supported tariff reviews and institutional strengthening across coastal and northeastern WSPs, while project management and technical assistance arrangements continue to provide effective oversight and coordination across all components.
